video_title: Stablecoins, Tokenization & the Future of Banking with Adam Nelson of FirstMark Capital
gist: FirstMark Capital fintech partner Adam Nelson argues to Dan Nathan that stable coins and tokenized real-world assets are a genuine platform shift on par with AI: roughly $300B issued today against a Treasury projection of $3 trillion within five years, with Circle and Tether already earning net income that would rank them the eighth largest US bank off treasury float. He maps where value accrues — issuer yield and the Clarity Act fight over on-chain yield, enterprise distribution via portfolio companies Rain and Velocity, and AI agents settling on stable coin rails — while arguing bank and card-network moats are weaker than consensus. Nathan presses on 24/7 tokenized equities, Hyperliquid's scale versus Robin Hood, and the convergence of betting, event contracts and equities into single apps.

themes.theme: Stable coins as the live platform shift

insights.claim: Roughly $300 billion of stable coins are issued today and stable coin transaction volumes already exceed the Visa and Mastercard networks, which Adam Nelson frames as still just a drop in the bucket.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: A base rate for sizing the theme: if on-chain volume already tops the card networks at $300B of float, the contested TAM is core money movement, not speculative crypto.
insights.quote: you're talking about $300 billion of of stable coins that are out in in uh in and issued. And you also have, you know, transaction volumes that are now kind of beyond the Visa and Mastercard networks

insights.claim: Sober legacy financial executives — not just founders — tell FirstMark that stable coins and tokenized real-world assets will change the core of the financial system, and when asked what inning adoption is in they answer that it is still spring training.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: If incumbents themselves put adoption before inning one, the repricing of settlement infrastructure is a multi-year runway rather than an already-crowded trade.
insights.quote: when I ask what inning are we in, they say we're in spring training

insights.claim: Stable coins are the first crypto product with a credible pitch to a non-crypto Fortune 100 CFO or bank — a dollar-pegged, treasury-backed instrument with 24/7 instant settlement at a fraction of traditional transaction cost — which is why crypto-summer/crypto-winter framing no longer governs adoption.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Decouple stable coin adoption from token price cycles; the demand driver is enterprise cost-of-settlement, not speculation.
insights.quote: there's this currency that's uh pegged to the US dollar. It is backed by US treasuries and it can be used for 247 instant settlement with a fraction of the transaction costs that exist in the traditional financial system

themes.theme: Incumbent moats: banks and the card networks

insights.claim: Adam Nelson believes too-big-to-fail bank moats are weaker than consensus assumes, because money is the ultimate network-effect business and as trust builds on chain incumbents must transform core business or bleed it away.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the durable-moat case behind large-cap bank multiples; track which institutions actually move core business on chain versus only announcing pilots.
insights.quote: I think the moes may be uh weaker than we think.

insights.claim: The most forward-thinking banks will pass stable coin settlement efficiency through to customers instead of defending fee income built on friction, shifting the model toward monetizing expertise and access.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Implies compression in fee lines that depend on payment friction, and a mix shift toward advisory and access-based revenue.
insights.quote: they don't want to make money on friction. They want to make money on their expertise and their access

insights.claim: Visa and Mastercard's vulnerability is cost, not speed — their pitch to merchants is instant guarantee and ubiquity, so the pressure point is how expensive the system is rather than settlement latency — and Nelson expects them to keep interchange, which he calls the price of admission, while using stable coin infrastructure to cut cost and free capital locked in prefunding.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Reframes the bear case on the networks: interchange compression is the wrong short thesis; lower cost structure and released prefunding capital could be margin-accretive.
insights.quote: Now, do I think they're going to get rid of their interchange fees? Absolutely not. That's uh I think that's price of admission

insights.claim: Customer inertia rather than product quality protects incumbent banks — NPS is mediocre and everyone complains, but nobody switches — so challengers win by bleeding away balances little by little until direct deposit and credit card payments migrate.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: The metric for fintech share gain is primary-account and direct-deposit migration, not funded accounts or downloads.
insights.quote: these have mediocre MPS, but people don't move

themes.theme: Issuer economics and the on-chain yield fight

insights.claim: Circle and Tether together would rank as roughly the eighth largest US bank by net income, earned by treating user balances as float and pushing reserves into treasuries to capture the spread.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Quantifies why every incumbent is launching a coin — issuer float economics already rival top-ten bank earnings with no credit book, and are a levered bet on front-end rates.
insights.quote: they're playing with your float while your money is in stable coins, which are effectively like your cash, your checking account, and they're pushing everything into uh into treasury and taking the spread

insights.claim: Whether yield can be delivered on chain alongside the dollar was left murky by existing regulation and is what the Clarity Act is trying to address; today it is not permitted.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: The largest single regulatory swing factor for issuer economics — permitting on-chain yield would compete away the treasury spread that funds issuer earnings.
insights.quote: the one thing that the regulation left pretty murky, which is what the Clarity Act is trying to uh address, is can you bring yield on chain

insights.claim: Because yield cannot be paid on chain, Circle instead routes a huge portion of its treasury yield to Coinbase as a customer acquisition cost so Coinbase members use Circle's stable coin.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Distribution, not issuance, captures the economics — whoever owns the customer extracts the yield, which is the template for bank and network coin launches.
insights.quote: that's why you have these arrangements like they have with Coinbase where they're basically paying a huge portion of the yield to Coinbase as a customer acquisition cost

insights.claim: Nelson describes Circle as an on-chain money market account masked as a stable coin, with a material counterparty delta versus Tether from US regulatory footprint and reserve transparency; breaking the buck is possible but would be a panic event rather than asset impairment.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Underwrite stable coin exposure as short-duration MMF risk: the tail is a run or confidence shock, so watch redemption behavior and attestation cadence, not the asset mix.
insights.quote: theoretically, could you break the buck? Yes, in the same way that money market funds theoretically can make break the buck, which is just a function of panic

themes.theme: Distribution plays: Rain, Velocity and enterprise adoption

insights.claim: Rain, a FirstMark portfolio company, is a stable coin-backed card issuer and a principal Visa member whose customer base has migrated from crypto exchanges to digital-first neo banks and now to large US financial institutions — the template adoption curve from crypto-native to mainstream.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: The stable coin spend layer is being built on top of the card networks rather than against them, and customer-mix migration to regulated FIs is the signal a company has crossed into the real TAM.

insights.claim: Nelson says Rain is growing as fast as any major AI company, putting stable coin payment infrastructure alongside AI as a private-market growth category.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Implies private capital will chase stable coin rails at AI-like valuations, with eventual IPO supply from the category.
insights.quote: that's a company that's growing, you know, as fast as any major AI company

insights.claim: FirstMark announced a Series A in Velocity, which works with merchants and acquirers as a full-stack enterprise stable coin solution — the mirror of Rain's issuer side — because today's stable coin tooling is developer primitives a Series B fintech can assemble but a Fortune 100 treasury spanning 80 global markets cannot.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: The bottleneck to enterprise adoption is packaging, not technology; full-stack vendors capture margin that developer-tool companies cannot.
insights.quote: If you're a Fortune 100 company trying to think about how to combine uh treasury operations across 80 different global markets, like forget about it.

insights.claim: Nelson cites Scott Bessent and the Treasury Department expecting three trillion dollars of stable coin issuance over the next five years, up from about $300 billion today, with ancillary revenue pools in FX and B2B payments on top.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: A 10x issuance path implies roughly $3T of incremental issuer demand for treasuries — a structural front-end bid and a policy motive for supporting the sector.
insights.quote: what the uh Scott Besson uh and the Treasury Department expect will be three trillion in stable coin issuance over the next 5 years

themes.theme: AI agents settling on stable coin rails

insights.claim: Nelson expects the vast majority of financial transactions to become humans instructing an AI agent, and argues agents will not place voice-authorized wires or use clunky legacy rails, so the always-on programmable instant-settlement stable coin layer becomes their default.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Frames agentic commerce as a direct demand driver for stable coin volume; whichever rail agents standardize on captures the transaction economics.

insights.claim: AI and stable coins are complementary rather than competing platform shifts — AI generates the interfaces from banking apps to ERP and becomes the coordination layer for payments, while stable coin rails deliver the value — but both are still very early.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Suggests the largest fintech outcomes sit at the AI-plus-stable coin intersection rather than in either category alone.
insights.quote: this is like peanut butter and jelly right now

insights.claim: Nelson's headline forecast is that in five to ten years the financial system will look entirely different, explicitly not tomorrow — a deliberately long-dated timeline for a shift he otherwise describes as already underway.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Calibrates horizon: this is a multi-year private-market compounding story, not a catalyst-driven public equity trade.
insights.quote: 5 10 years from now you're going to wake up and everything we know about the financial system is going to look uh entirely different

themes.theme: Tokenizing stocks and the end of the 9:30-to-4 market

insights.claim: The case for tokenizing equities is operational rather than about price discovery: stocks trade roughly 8-to-5 instead of 24/7, collateral settles over multiple days instead of immediately, and moving a position between brokers requires ACAT paperwork that tokenization removes.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Points the disruption at custody, clearing, transfer agents and the intermediaries paid for paperwork, not at exchange matching engines.
insights.quote: right now stocks trade 85 instead of 247

insights.claim: Tokenization extends beyond equities to money market funds and bonds, where Nelson expects on-chain versions to unlock far more functionality, notably instant collateral delivery and lending without weeks of paperwork.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Collateral mobility is the killer app for RWA tokenization; prime brokerage and securities lending economics are the pressure point.

insights.claim: Dan Nathan counters that off-hours equity trading carries real risks — poor liquidity, limited transparency and unknown counterparties at 3pm on a Saturday — while conceding most volume still occurs in normal hours.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Execution quality in 24/7 tokenized venues is the underpriced risk; thin off-hours books are where retail gets adversely selected.

themes.theme: Hyperliquid, prediction markets and the everything-app for money

insights.claim: Hyperliquid, the largest perpetual-futures decentralized exchange, is about 80% the size of Robin Hood's crypto and equity businesses combined while running with roughly 12 employees, and is not available to US investors.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: An offshore 12-person venue at 80% of Robin Hood's scale is a direct read on how much order flow US-regulated brokers are already ceding.
insights.quote: we we just looked it's about 80% of the size of uh Robin Hood if you combine their crypto and equity

insights.claim: Offshore perp exchanges and prediction markets are becoming price-discovery venues: Nelson says IPO desks keep Hyperliquid open to manage pricing on pre-listing names, the same way Kalshi and Polymarket became indicative for mayoral elections and the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: These venues are effectively a free reference-price feed for pre-IPO and event exposure that traditional desks are already consuming.

insights.claim: Nelson argues US institutions cannot opt out of decentralized perp exchanges and prediction markets because nobody can turn Hyperliquid off, so the real work is solving KYC and AML integration rather than debating whether 24/7 trading should exist.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Expect US brokers and regulators to move toward accommodation; the compliance-wrapper layer over offshore venues is an investable gap.
insights.quote: no one's turning Hyperliquid off and it's now almost as big as Robin Hood

insights.claim: Nelson expects sports betting, event contracts, equities and crypto to converge into single apps, leaving brand affinity — not product exclusivity — as the durable moat for Kalshi, Polymarket, Robin Hood and Wealthfront, with Robin Hood's 27-28 million funded accounts as the beachhead.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Pure-play betting and prediction operators face funnel competition from already-funded brokerage accounts; bundling favors the everything-app.
insights.quote: why wouldn't your sports betting and your uh and your futures contract and your equity and your crypto all stay in one place?

insights.claim: The entire fintech sector is less than 1% of global banking, stocks and brokerage, which Nelson uses as the sizing argument for why share-taking from incumbents remains the profit pool worth attacking.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Frames fintech penetration from a sub-1% base, implying the constraint is distribution and inertia rather than addressable market.
insights.quote: the entire fintech sector is less than 1% of global banking and and uh and stocks and brokerage etc.

insights.claim: With hindsight, the right 2023 fintech move was not hunting new categories but doubling and tripling down on winners built in the back half of the 2010s — Stripe, Revolut and emerging names like Ramp — which defined value creation through the interim period.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: In a post-shift lull, concentration in proven category leaders beats new-category exploration — a reusable allocation rule between cycles.
insights.quote: the thing to have done in, you know, 2023 was just to look at the winners who had been built in uh, you know, the back half of the 2010s and just continue to to double and triple down on them

insights.claim: Public fintech CEOs face a two-front problem — setting a stable coin and tokenization strategy for a shift that has not hit yet but will over the next five years, while simultaneously integrating AI, which Nelson frames as either a large revenue and cost benefit or the thing that kills them.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: A screening lens for public fintech names: management teams without a credible answer on both stable coins and AI are the vulnerable cohort.
insights.quote: this might not have hit me yet, but it's about to hit me over the next 5 years when this stuff goes mainstream
